                                          I.     INTRODUCTION

        Kevin Kennedy (“Mr. Kennedy”), retired professional engineer, landowner, and pro se

intervenor, respectfully files this Reply Brief on Remand of Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and

13 to the State Office of Administrative Hearings ("SOAH") Administrative Law Judges

("ALJs") regarding Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (“Oncor’s”) and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation’s (“LCRA’s”) (collectively, “Applicants”) application to

amend a certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) for the Bell County East to Big Hill

765-kV transmission line (“59475”). The Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”)

remanded only those two issues to SOAH for further consideration. 1

        The 59475 proceedings were consolidated by SOAH to the extent necessary to address

common need issues with Applicants’ Big Hill to Sand Lake 765-kV transmission line

(“59182”). This brief addresses reliability issues in both 59475 and 59182.

        The ALJs ordered briefing on the existing evidentiary record and directed that factual

assertions include specific record citations. This reply brief addresses Issue 11, and the

engineering foundation of the Applicants’ asserted reliability need. 2 3

       II.     SUMMARY

            Issue 11 cannot be answered in the affirmative without qualified underlying engineering

studies. The study reports referenced by the Applicants, completed by the Electric Reliability

Council of Texas. Inc. (“ERCOT”), a private corporation, do not carry a professional engineer’s

seal. There can only be a few reasons why ERCOT and the 25-30 professional engineers they

employ would not seal their studies. Some possible examples may be:

                a) Maybe ERCOT considers their work too basic or rudimentary to call it
                   engineering. Maybe it’s just a best guess type effort, in their professional
                   judgment.
                b) Maybe it is engineering but is not of a good enough caliber so that any ERCOT
                   professional engineer was willing to put their seal and signature on it.
                c) Maybe ERCOT and their professional engineers believe they are exempt from the
                   Texas Engineering Practice Act (“TEPA”), for reasons currently unknown.

            If ERCOT just “winged it”, the Commission cannot rely on that work for the basis of

proof of need. If it is engineering, why did no engineer seal it?


            Mr. Kennedy, a retired professional engineer, considers ERCOT’s studies to be

engineering as defined by TEPA, though he has questioned the validity of some of their key

modeling decisions. Additionally, Mr. Kennedy does not find an apparent TEPA exemption

applicable to ERCOT. As such, Mr. Kennedy believes that it is not unreasonable to find that

ERCOT and its professional engineers are in violation of TEPA. Further, TEPA requires that

public officials shall report a violation of TEPA for investigation. 4 Mr. Kennedy notifies the

ALJs, the Commission, and the PUC staff engineers, as public officials, of their duty to report

the lack of an engineer’s seal on the numerous ERCOT’s studies referenced in this docket.


            Determining whether an interconnected transmission grid meets federal reliability

standards established by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) requires


4
    Tex. Occ. Code §1001.553.

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                            Page 4 of 13
 complex power-flow calculations, stability modeling, short-circuit studies, and contingency

analysis.


          The NERC standards most relevant to the engineering required to prove necessity of

59475 are:

                 TPL-001-5.1: Transmission system planning performance requirements


                 MOD-032-1: Data for power system modeling and analysis


                 MOD-033-2: Steady-state and dynamic system model validation


          The necessary engineering analysis applies electrical engineering principles to predict

how the ERCOT grid system will perform under normal conditions and after equipment failures.

That work is defined as engineering under TEPA.5


          ERCOT performed engineering work in preparing the reports on which Applicants rely:

the PBRP 6, 2024 RTP 7, 2024 RTP 345-kV and 765-kV Plan Comparison 8, and 2025 RTP 9.

TEPA does not exempt ERCOT or this work from its firm registration or sealing requirements.

The reports are not sealed by a professional engineer. ERCOT’s firm registration number is not

noted on the reports. The Commission must reject them as the basis for qualified engineering

approval, deny the applications for failure to prove need, and refer this TEPA violation matter to

TBPELS for investigation.10

                     III.   ARGUMENT - PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11

             Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability
             standards?

     A. ERCOT’s recommendation does not settle the need for this line.

              The Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) requires a finding that the requested

     facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

     The Commission rules give ERCOT’s reliability assessment “great weight.” Yet “great

     weight” is not irrebuttable weight. Determination of compliance with federal standards

     requires complex engineering analysis. Affording “great weight” to ERCOT does not

     eliminate the necessity for an ERCOT engineering examination of the scope, case

     assumptions, study year, contingency results, or causal link between an identified violation

     and a build/no-build analysis of the proposed project. 11 Qualified engineering work must

     comply with TEPA; a failing negates the work’s merit. 12

              Applicants must connect the claimed reliability need to the discreet 59475 facilities

     they seek to build. That requires an engineering explanation of the study assumptions, the

     violations without the project, and how the project corrects the violation.


     B. Applicants acknowledge the PBRP’s limited purpose.

              In responding to Mr. Kennedy’s appeal of SOAH Order No. 35, Applicants asserted:

     “Special ERCOT studies like the PBRP are not required to, and generally are not intended to,

     independently demonstrate compliance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1.” They

     described the PBRP as a special-purpose study responsive to H.B. 5066. 13




11
     Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c), (c-1), (d); 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II).
12
     Tex. Occ. Code §§1001.402; 1001.553.
13
     Applicants’ Response to Kevin Kennedy’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 35 at 8, PUC Docket No. 59475, Item
     6610 (Sept. 30, 2026).

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                Page 6 of 13
      C. NERC compliance requires engineering analysis.

              TPL-001-5.1 requires system models and planning assessments supported by steady-

     state, short-circuit, and stability analyses. MOD-032 governs modeling data, and MOD-033

     governs model validation. This work requires engineering judgment. 14

              The PBRP considered only 345-kV import paths for 2030 case studies with limited

     evaluation of 765-kV import paths for the 2038 forecast cases. Applicants must explain how

     the 345-kV work proves the claimed reliability violation need for the 59475 765-kV. 15


     D. Studying the three PBRP import lines together does not establish this line’s need.

              Applicants’ professional engineer witness Gurley was not aware of a study that

     isolated each 765-kV line independently. The three import lines were studied together.

     Applicants must connect their claim to the particular 59475 facilities requested here. A

     recommendation for three import paths does not itself establish the necessity of Bell County

     East–Big Hill to cure violation of a state or federal standard. 16

              The 2024 RTP 765-kV starting case already included all three PBRP import paths.

     The 2025 RTP included the 765-kV STEP in its 2030 and 2031 starting cases. Showing how

     a system performs with the proposed facilities does not, in itself, establish why those

     facilities are necessary. Applicants must explain the comparison of a validated system model

     with and without an isolated 59475. 17




14
     NERC TPL-001-5.1, R1–R4; MOD-032-1, R1–R4; MOD-033-2, R1–R2. These standards govern the identified
     functional entities; they do not themselves prescribe Texas professional-engineer seals.

     (Item 6593).

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                      Page 7 of 13
                The 2024 RTP reported similar key reliability needs after reducing forecasted load.

     That result may speak to ERCOT’s broader reliability concern. It does not explain which

     results establish the need for this particular line.18


     E. The different model inputs require an explanation.

                   Applicants admitted response calls the STEP (i.e. 2024 RTP) and PBRP load

          cases “separate and distinct cases.” Was the PBRP load case accurate? Did the spatial and

          temporal differences in load demand and generation supply in the two models affect the

          model output. Applicants must explain how those different cases establish the need for

          Import Path 2. 19


     F. General planning benefits do not prove the claimed reliability need.

               Applicants rely on studies with different assumptions and starting networks. They

     must show how those studies establish the need for the requested facilities under a state or

     federal reliability standard. General benefits from arbitrarily adding transmission

     infrastructure do not answer that question.



               The Commission should answer Issue 11 in the negative, based on the existing

     record.

                                  IV.     FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH TEPA

     A. ERCOT performed engineering work and TEPA applies.

               ERCOT performed engineering work. Section 1001.003(b) and (c)(1), (2), (6), and

     (10) covers engineering analysis, planning, studies, conceptual design, and electrical utility

     systems. ERCOT modeled the grid, analyzed contingencies, compared transmission

     alternatives, and recommended identified facilities. Those activities meet the statutory

     definition of engineering. 20

               ERCOT calls the PBRP a “significant engineering effort” involving “extensive

     engineering analysis.” The RTPs and comparison report also analyze transmission facilities.

     Calling this work “planning” does not remove it from TEPA. 21

               Nothing in TEPA exempts ERCOT’s preparation and public issuance of these reports

     from the sealing requirements. ERCOT’s reports recommend grid projects to be built by

     others. Section 1001.058 is a limited licensing exemption for certain utility employees. It

     excludes final authority or ultimate responsibility for engineering plans made public or

     incorporated into systems on others’ property. 22


     B. The Commission must reject the unsealed studies.

               Section 1001.052 permits subordinate employees to work under an engineer without

     individual licenses. It does not excuse the responsible engineer. Section 1001.051 limits

     Subchapter B exemptions to persons who do not offer engineering services to the public. The




20
     Tex. Occ. Code §1001.003(b), (c)(1), (2), (6), (10); Applicants’ Ex. 3, Ex. JG-2, pp. 6–9 of 82; Ex. JG-4, pp. 11–
     28 of 40; Applicants’ Ex. 17, Ex. JG-R-2, pp. 33–34 of 44; Ex. JG-R-3, p. 28 of 58.
21
     Applicants’ Ex. 3, Ex. JG-2, p. 1 of 82 (ERCOT transmittal letter) and p. 6 of 82 (executive summary);
     Applicants’ Ex. 17, Ex. JG-R-2, p. 2 of 44, and Ex. JG-R-3, p. 2 of 58.
22
     Tex. Occ. Code §1001.058(a)(1)–(2). Section 1001.058 is an employee licensing exemption; it does not establish
     a blanket exemption for a utility-related corporation.

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                         Page 9 of 13
      remaining exemptions do not cover these reports. ERCOT’s statutory planning assignment

     creates no TEPA exemption.23

              Section 1001.401(b) requires an engineer’s seal on a report issued by a license holder

     for a Texas project. Rule 137.33(f)(2) requires a seal and signature on a bound engineering

     report’s original title sheet; subsection (k) also requires seals on reports for Texas projects.

     These reports support construction of the identified 59475 transmission facilities. They are

     project engineering reports. 24

          Rule 137.33(f)(3) treats other work, including research, recommendations, and litigation

documents, differently. It does not displace the requirements for project engineering reports

under (f)(2) and (k). The public-employee provision in subsection (h) concerns specified

compliance reviews and general planning documents. It does not excuse the original project

engineering reports used here.25

          The four ERCOT reports in the record do not bear a professional engineer’s seal. Section

1001.402 permits a public official responsible for enforcing laws affecting engineering to accept

a plan, specification, or related document only when an engineer’s seal evidences its preparation

by an engineer. The Commission enforces Texas laws, including ERCOT engineering reliability

work under the State statute of Utilities Code §39.151(d). The Commission must reject these

unsealed reports as the engineering basis for approval. 26

          “Great weight” under a Commission administrative rule cannot override the

Commission’s statutory duty under §39.151(d) and §1001.402.




23
     Tex. Occ. Code §§1001.051–.068; Tex. Util. Code §§39.151, 39.167. Section 1001.052 concerns employees or
     subordinates of a licensed engineer who do not exercise responsible charge.
24
     Tex. Occ. Code §1001.401(b), (d); 22 Tex. Admin. Code §137.33(f)(1)–(2), (k), (m). Sealing exemptions depend
     on an applicable statutory exemption.
25
     22 Tex. Admin. Code §137.33(f)(2)–(3), (h), (k). Kennedy seeks treatment of these documents as original project
     engineering reports, rather than the other work or public-employee reviews described in the cited provisions.
26
     Tex. Occ. Code §§1001.002(2), 1001.402; Tex. Util. Code §39.151(d); Applicants’ Ex. 3, Exs. JG-2 and JG-4;
     Applicants’ Ex. 17, Exs. JG-R-2 and JG-R-3 (report title pages and complete reports).

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                     Page 10 of 13
            Applicants’ engineering testimony does not supply the missing seals or close the gaps in

their proof of this line’s necessity. Without the ERCOT reports, Applicants have offered no proof

of the required reliability need. 27

           Section 1001.553 requires public officials to report TEPA violations. The Commission

must refer ERCOT’s preparation and issuance of these unsealed engineering reports to TBPELS

for investigation.

           The ALJs may not have authority to order a Commission audit of the ERCOT modeling,

but they have authority to recommend it. The ALJs’ PFD should recommend a Commission

order for technical investigation and audit of ERCOT studies and also recommend Commission

referral of TEPA violations to TBPELS. Further, as public officials, the ALJs should report the

TEPA violation themselves. TBPELS should investigate compliance with TEPA regarding

responsibility for the work and with the firm-registration requirements of §1001.405. 28 29



           The Commission must answer Issue 11 in the negative and deny the applications.



      V.        PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT, CONCLUSIONS OF LAW, AND ORDERS

     A. Proposed Findings of Fact.

           1.   ERCOT performed grid modeling, contingency analysis, and transmission planning
                in preparing the PBRP, 2024 RTP, 2024 RTP 345-kV and 765-kV Plan Comparison,
                and 2025 RTP.30

           2.   Applicants rely on the ERCOT reports in the record to support the reliability need for
                the proposed facilities.31

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Brief on Remand of Issues 11 and 13                                       Page 11 of 13
           3.   The copies of the ERCOT reports in the evidentiary record do not bear a professional
               engineer’s seal or an ERCOT engineering firm registration number. 32

          4.   No Subchapter B exemption excuses ERCOT’s engineering work.

          5.   The ALJs, Commission, and PUC staff professional engineers are public officials.

          6.   Without an engineer’s seal or a firm registration number, the Commission may not
               accept ERCOT’s PBRP, 2024 RTP, 2024 RTP 345-kV and 765-kV Plan
               Comparison, and 2025 RTP. 33

     B. Proposed Conclusions of Law.

          1.   ERCOT’s preparation of these reports is engineering under Tex. Occ. Code
               §1001.003(b) and (c)(1), (2), (6), and (10).

          2.   ERCOT is in violation of TEPA.

          3.   Sections 1001.401(b) and 1001.402 require rejection of the unsealed reports as the
               engineering basis for approval. Applicants have failed to prove necessity under Issue
               11.34

          7.   Tex. Occ. Code §1001.553 requires the ALJs, Commission, and PUC staff
               professional engineers to report the TEPA violations to TBPELS for investigation.
               The Commission remains responsible for deciding the CCN applications. 35

     C. Proposed Orders.

          4.   The 59182 and 59475 applications to amend CCNs are denied.

          5.   ERCOT TEPA violations shall be referred to TBPELS.



                                    VI.     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

          ERCOT performed engineering work. TEPA does not exempt this work. The four reports

are not sealed by an engineer and cannot supply the engineering basis for approval under

§1001.402. Applicants have failed to prove the required reliability need. The Commission must

                                          I.      INTRODUCTION

        Kevin Kennedy ("Mr. Kennedy"), retired professional engineer, landowner, and pro se

intervenor, respectfully files this Reply Brief on Remand of Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and

13 to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (" SOAH") Administrative Law Judges

("ALJs") regarding Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLCU ("Oncor , " ) and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation' s ("LCRA's") (collectively, "Applicants") application to

amend a certificate of convenience and necessity ("CCN") for the Bell County East to Big Hill

765-kV transmission line ("59475"). The Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission")

remanded only those two issues to SOAH for further consideration. 1

     II.      SUMMARY

          Issue 11 cannot be answered in the affirmative without qualified underlying engineering

studies. The study reports referenced by the Applicants, completed by the Electric Reliability

Council of Texas. Inc. ("ERCOT"), a private corporation, do not carry a professional engineer' s

seal. There can only be a few reasons why ERCOT and the 25-30 professional engineers they

employ would not seal their studies. Some possible examples may be:

              a) Maybe ERCOT considers their work too basic or rudimentary to call it
                  engineering. Maybe it' s just a best guess type effort, in their professional
                 judgment.
              b) Maybe it is engineering but is not of a good enough caliber so that any ERCOT
                 professional engineer was willing to put their seal and signature on it.
              c) Maybe ERCOT and their professional engineers believe they are exempt from the
                 Texas Engineering Practice Act ("TEPA"), for reasons currently unknown.

          IfERCOT just "winged it", the Commission cannot rely on that work forthe basis of

proof of need. If it is engineering, why did no engineer seal it?


          Mr. Kennedy, a retired professional engineer, considers ERCOT's studies to be

engineering as defined by TEPA, though he has questioned the validity of some of their key

modeling decisions. Additionally, Mr. Kennedy does not find an apparent TEPA exemption

applicable to ERCOT. As such, Mr. Kennedy believes that it is not unreasonable to find that

ERCOT and its professional engineers are in violation of TEPA. Further, TEPA requires that

public officials shall report a violation of TEPA for investigation. 4 Mr. Kennedy notifies the

ALJs, the Commission, and the PUC staff engineers, as public officials, of their duty to report

the lack of an engineer' s seal on the numerous ERCOT's studies referenced in this docket.


          Determining whether an interconnected transmission grid meets federal reliability

standards established by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ("NERC") requires

           Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability
           standards?

    A. ERCOT's recommendation does not settle the need for this line.

             The Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA") requires a finding that the requested

    facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

    The Commission rules give ERCOT' s reliability assessment "great weight." Yet "great

    weight" is not irrebuttable weight. Determination of compliance with federal standards

    requires complex engineering analysis. Affording "great weight" to ERCOT does not

    eliminate the necessity for an ERCOT engineering examination of the scope, case

    assumptions, study year, contingency results, or causal link between an identified violation

    and a build/no-build analysis of the proposed project. 11 Qualified engineering work must

    comply with TEPA; a failing negates the work' s merit. 12

                               IV.     FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH TEPA

    A. ERCOT performed engineering work and TEPA applies.

             ERCOT performed engineering work. Section 1001.003(b) and (c)(1), (2), (6), and

    (10) covers engineering analysis, planning, studies, conceptual design, and electrical utility

    systems. ERCOT modeled the grid, analyzed contingencies, compared transmission

    alternatives, and recommended identified facilities. Those activities meet the statutory

    definition of engineering. 20

             ERCOT calls the PBRP a "significant engineering effort" involving "extensive

    engineering analysis." The RTPs and comparison report also analyze transmission facilities.

    Calling this work "planning" does not remove it from TEPA. 21

             Nothing in TEPA exempts ERCOT' s preparation and public issuance of these reports

    from the sealing requirements. ERCOT' s reports recommend grid projects to be built by

    others. Section 1001.058 is a limited licensing exemption for certain utility employees. It

    excludes final authority or ultimate responsibility for engineering plans made public or

    incorporated into systems on others' property. 22


    B. The Commission must reject the unsealed studies.

             Section 1001.052 permits subordinate employees to work under an engineer without

    individual licenses. It does not excuse the responsible engineer. Section 1001.051 limits

    Subchapter B exemptions to persons who do not offer engineering services to the public. The
